title: AI-LIGHTS: AI-assisted Long-read Genomics and Integrated OMICs for Healthcare Solutions
summary: In some critically ill children, the cause of their condition remains unclear despite extensive diagnostic testing. A rare genetic disorder may be responsible. AI-LIGHTS combines modern genetic testing with additional molecular analyses. In addition to genome sequencing, the study investigates long DNA molecules, gene activity, proteins, and metabolic products. Computer-based and AI-assisted methods are used to analyze these different types of information together. The study examines whether this approach can identify the cause of disease in more children and whether the results are useful for diagnosis and clinical care. It also assesses how quickly results become available, what additional information each method contributes, and how parents perceive the benefit of the diagnostic process. The study does not assign experimental treatments; medical decisions remain with the treating physicians.
conditions: Critical illness in childhood with suspected rare or genetic etiology

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1) Critically ill child without an etiological diagnosis who has not yet reached 14 years of age. 2) A well-founded clinical suspicion of an underlying rare disease or rare genetic disorder as the cause of the critical illness. 3) Inpatient treatment in a neonatal or pediatric intensive care unit (NICU or PICU) at Hannover Medical School.
Exclusion criteria:
1) A known cause of disease that satisfactorily explains the child's symptoms. 2) One of the common chromosomal disorders (trisomy 13, 18, or 21, or Turner syndrome) is considered in the differential diagnosis and has not yet been excluded by appropriate diagnostic testing. 3) A blood transfusion has taken place within the preceding 48 hours. Inclusion is possible after this interval; alternatively, a saliva sample may be collected. The treating physicians and the principal investigator decide which approach is used. 4) The principal investigator determines that study participation is not in the participant's best interest, for example when another diagnostic test is more likely to establish the diagnosis. Later inclusion may be reconsidered in an interdisciplinary case conference.
